payload.name: wavelet-packet
payload.scope: A human-made signal decomposition method that generalizes the wavelet transform by decomposing both approximation and detail subbands at each tree level, producing a complete binary tree of subband representations. Unlike the standard wavelet transform that only recursively decomposes the approximation branch, the wavelet-packet algorithm applies the same decomposition to every node, enabling optimal basis selection for signal-specific energy concentration.

definition.body: A signal decomposition algorithm that recursively partitions a signal into subbands using a binary tree structure. At each node, both the low-frequency (approximation) and high-frequency (detail) outputs are further decomposed by a pair of quadrature mirror filters followed by downsampling. The algorithm is parameterized by: (1) the maximum decomposition depth (number of tree levels), (2) the wavelet basis function (e.g., Daubechies, Haar, Coiflet) defining the filter coefficients, (3) the node selection criteria (e.g., best-first, bottom-up, or exhaustive search over the full tree), and (4) the cost function for optimal basis selection (commonly Shannon entropy of subband energies). The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: the method is implemented in DSP libraries (MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox, Python PyWavelets, librosa) and taught in signal processing curricula. e.g.: MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox wavedec2 function; PyWavelets pywt.wavedec with full tree decomposition; librosa.feature.melspectrogram using packet decomposition for audio feature extraction | not: standard discrete wavelet transform (only approximations decomposed, not the full tree) [formal: transformatio pacellae waveleticae | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: gabor-transform
payload.scope: A human-made time-frequency analysis method that computes the short-time Fourier transform using a fixed Gaussian window function. Introduced by Dennis Gabor in 1946 as a 'deterministic uncertainty principle' for signal analysis, it produces a complex-valued representation of signal energy localized in both time and frequency. Unlike the general STFT where window shape and width are free parameters, the Gabor transform uses a specifically Gaussian window whose width parameter sigma controls the time-frequency resolution trade-off.

definition.body: A time-frequency representation defined by G(tau, omega) = integral from -inf to +inf of f(t) * exp(-(t-tau)^2/(2*sigma^2)) * exp(-i*omega*t) dt, where sigma is the Gaussian window width parameter controlling the time-frequency resolution trade-off. Parameters: (1) sigma — the standard deviation of the Gaussian window, determining the fixed time-frequency resolution bandwidth (Heisenberg box size = sigma * (1/(4*pi*sigma))), (2) the time and frequency sampling step sizes for discrete computation. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic and theoretical: implemented in MATLAB (gabor), Python (scipy.signal.gaussian for window generation), and image processing toolboxes; foundational to squeezed-state quantum mechanics and the Gabor frame theory of Daubechies, Grossmann, and Meyer. e.g.: MATLAB gabor function for image feature extraction; Python librosa.feature.melspectrogram using fixed Gaussian windows; Daubechies Grossmann Meyer Gabor frame theory in applied harmonic analysis textbooks | not: short-time Fourier transform with non-Gaussian window (e.g., rectangular, Hanning, Blackman windows) [formal: gaboriana transformatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: autocorrelation-method
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing method for estimating autoregressive model parameters from a finite signal segment by computing autocorrelation lags and solving the resulting Toeplitz system, producing a guaranteed-stable all-pole filter model.

definition.body: The autocorrelation method estimates autoregressive model parameters by computing autocorrelation lags of a finite-length signal segment, forming a symmetric Toeplitz system of equations, and solving for prediction coefficients that minimize the forward prediction error energy under the assumption that signal values outside the analysis window are zero. The method computes r(k) = sum_{n=0}^{N-1-k} x[n]x[n+k] for k=0..p, then solves the Toeplitz system R·a = r where R is the autocorrelation matrix. Unlike the covariance method, it pads the data with zeros outside the window, yielding a guaranteed-stable filter. Parameters: prediction order p, signal segment x[n] of length N. Persistence mechanism: standard in spectral estimation texts (e.g., Stoica Moses Spectral Analysis, Chapter 5), implemented in MATLAB's pburg as the default autocorrelation approach, embedded in spectral analysis toolkits. e.g.: computing 11th-order AR model of a 200-sample speech frame in MATLAB's aryule function; forming the autocorrelation Toeplitz matrix for spectral estimation in the Kaldi PLP pipeline; estimating AR coefficients for spectrogram inversion using zero-padded autocorrelation in Python's scipy; the covariance-based AR model in Praat speech analysis tool where the autocorrelation window is applied | not: the covariance method (uses data only within the window without zero-padding, yielding a non-Toeplitz system); the Burg method (minimizes forward and backward prediction error power with reflection coefficient constraint); Yule-Walker equations (the formalism R·a=r, not the autocorrelation data method) [formal: methodus autocorrelationis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: mel-frequency-warping
payload.scope: A human-made frequency warping technique that maps linear frequency to a perceptually motivated mel scale, used to model human auditory perception in speech and audio processing. Persisted through standardization in MFCC computation and audio codec design.

definition.body: Mel-frequency warping is a nonlinear mapping from linear frequency f (Hz) to mel scale m = 2595 log10(1 + f/700). Parameters: warping formula, center frequencies of filterbanks, number of filters. Persistence mechanism: encoded in speech recognition pipelines (HTK, Kaldi, librosa), audio codecs, and psychoacoustic models. e.g.: mel filterbank in MFCC computation; mel-scale spectrogram in librosa.feature.melspectrogram; warping in MPEG-7 audio descriptors | not: linear frequency scaling (a simple multiplication); constant-Q transform (log-frequency but with different basis) [formal: warping mel-frequency | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

The board already holds harmonicity (general) and source-harmonicity (voice) as the named constructs; a renamed, rescaled re-parameterization of the same harmonic-to-residual ratio is a duplicate, not a new construct. The scope's own 'binary classification cue between tonal and noise segments' is the same purpose harmonicity serves. STRIKE on item 4.

payload.name: z-transform
payload.scope: People made the z-transform to analyze discrete-time signals and digital filters in the frequency domain, so that difference equations and digital filter design could be handled by the same algebraic, pole-zero methods used for continuous systems.

definition.body: The z-transform is a human-made mathematical operation that maps a discrete-time sequence x[n] to a function of the complex variable z, defined as the bilateral sum X(z) = Σ x[n]·z^(−n) over all integers n (or the unilateral sum over n ≥ 0). Parameters: (1) the sequence x[n] to be transformed; (2) the region of convergence (ROC) in the z-plane, the set of z for which the sum converges; (3) the pole and zero locations giving the closed rational form of X(z) for rational sequences. It is the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform, obtained by the sampled-data substitution z = e^(sT) with sampling period T, and it turns difference equations into algebraic equations in z so that stability (poles inside the unit circle) and the frequency response (X(z) evaluated on the unit circle z = e^(jωT)) are read directly from the pole-zero pattern. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the central transform of digital signal processing, codified in transform tables and operational rules, implemented in analysis tools (MATLAB's tf2zp and zplane, the z-transform routines of Oppenheim's DSP toolchain), and taught as a standard step of DSP curricula. e.g.: the z-transform of the unit step u[n] giving X(z)=1/(1−z^(−1)) in Oppenheim & Schafer's Discrete-Time Signal Processing; pole-zero placement of a digital IIR filter in the z-plane per Proakis & Manolakis Digital Signal Processing; MATLAB tf2zp converting a transfer function to z-plane zeros, poles and gain | not: the discrete-time Fourier transform (the z-transform evaluated on the unit circle); the Laplace transform (the continuous-time analog, not the z-plane object) [formal: transformatio zetae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: discrete-time-fourier-transform
payload.scope: People made the discrete-time Fourier transform to read the frequency content of an infinite discrete sequence as a continuous, periodic function of real frequency, so that LTI system analysis and the sampling relation of the DFT could be stated without the finite-grid aliasing of the DFT itself.

definition.body: The discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT) is a human-made mathematical operation that maps a discrete-time sequence x[n] to a continuous, 2π-periodic function of real frequency ω, defined as the bilateral sum X(e^(jω)) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n]·e^(−jωn) over all integers n. Parameters: (1) the sequence x[n] to be transformed; (2) the real frequency ω; (3) the summation convention — bilateral over all integers, or the unilateral variant over n ≥ 0. The DTFT is the continuous-frequency object of which the DFT is a sampling: the DFT of an N-length sequence samples the DTFT at ω = 2πk/N for k = 0..N−1, and the DTFT equals the z-transform evaluated on the unit circle z = e^(jω). It turns convolution into pointwise multiplication and reads the frequency response H(e^(jω)) of a linear time-invariant system directly from the transform of its impulse response. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard continuous-frequency analysis of discrete sequences, codified in transform tables and the DTFT chapters of the DSP textbooks, and implemented in the frequency-response computations of MATLAB's freqz and in DSP curricula worldwide. e.g.: the Dirichlet-kernel DTFT of a rectangular window in Oppenheim & Schafer's Discrete-Time Signal Processing; the H(e^(jω)) of a digital IIR filter from its impulse response in Proakis & Manolakis; freqz of the MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox | not: the discrete Fourier transform (finite N-point sampling of this continuous transform); the continuous-time Fourier transform (integral over real time, not a sum over samples) [formal: transformatio Fourier temporalis discreta | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

replacementSpec.body: Cepstral-domain is the human-made practice and tooling for representing signals in a log-spectral inverse Fourier space for cepstral analysis. It is a made analytical framework consisting of: (1) a specification for computing a log-magnitude spectrum of a windowed frame; (2) a defined inverse Fourier transform step that maps that log spectrum to quefrency samples; (3) conventions for interpreting those samples as cepstral coefficients, including quefrency axis labeling, liftering, and coefficient indexing. Parameters: window length and type, FFT size, overlap, liftering cutoff, number of coefficients retained. Persistence mechanism: maintained as documented procedures in speech processing standards, implemented in libraries (librosa, speechpy, Kaldi), taught in DSP curricula, and used in deployed codecs and recognizers. e.g.: the cepstral-domain implementation in librosa.feature.mfcc that computes log mel-spectrum and inverse DCT; the quefrency-domain representation used in ITU-T G.729 pitch estimation; the cepstral liftering step in Kaldi's MFCC feature pipeline; the log-spectrum to cepstrum conversion in the Voice Activity Detection module of WebRTC | not: the raw frequency domain (FFT magnitude without log); the time domain (original waveform samples); the power spectrum (pre-log representation) [formal: dominium cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.note: DERIVED_FROM [3 test; 2 direction] Laplace transform (developed by Euler and Laplace in the 1780s) predates the bilinear transform (mid-20th century). The bilinear transform was developed specifically to convert analog filter prototypes expressed in the Laplace domain H(s) into discrete-time z-domain implementations H(z). payload.name: partial-autocorrelation
payload.scope: People made the partial autocorrelation to measure direct linear dependence between time series observations at a given lag, removing the confounding influence of all shorter lags, enabling model order identification in AR analysis.

definition.body: A partial autocorrelation at lag k is a human-made statistical measure quantifying the direct linear relationship between two samples of a stationary time series separated by k steps, after removing the linear influence of all intermediate samples at lags 1 through k−1. Parameters: (1) the time series data or the underlying process; (2) the lag k, a positive integer; (3) the method of computation — solving the Yule-Walker equations via Levinson-Durbin recursion, or equivalently via autoregressive model fitting. The partial autocorrelation at lag k equals the last coefficient φ_kk of an AR(k) model fitted to the data, and equals zero for k greater than the true AR order when the process is truly AR(p). Persistence mechanism: computed by statistical libraries (scipy, R stats), visualized in PACF plots for time-series model identification, and taught in time-series analysis textbooks (Box-Jenkins methodology, Hamilton Time Series Analysis). e.g.: PACF of an AR(2) simulated time series showing spike only at lags 1 and 2; PACF plot from R stats acf function for identifying AR order in economic data; scipy.linalg.solve computing AR coefficients for partial autocorrelation at lag 5; R pacf function applied to ACF data to extract partial autocorrelations | not: autocorrelation at lag k (measures total correlation including indirect effects through intermediate lags, not partial); cross-correlation (measures relationship between two different series, not within one series) [formal: partialis correlatio autocorrelationis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-factorization
payload.scope: People made spectral factorization to decompose a power spectral density into minimum-phase and maximum-phase filter components, enabling causal filter design from spectral specifications.

definition.body: A spectral factorization is a human-made mathematical procedure that decomposes a power spectral density S(e^(jω)) into the squared magnitude response of a rational transfer function H(z), such that S(z) = H(z)·H(z^(-1)) evaluated on the unit circle. Parameters: (1) the power spectral density or its rational z-domain representation S(z) with symmetric poles and zeros; (2) the choice of factor — minimum-phase (all poles and zeros inside the unit circle for stability and causality), maximum-phase, or mixed-phase. The procedure assigns poles and zeros: those inside the unit circle go to H(z) for minimum-phase, outside for the conjugate factor. Persistence mechanism: implemented in DSP libraries for Wiener filter design, used in speech processing for inverse filter computation from LPC spectrum, and taught in signal processing textbooks (Oppenheim and Schafer, Proakis). e.g.: MATLAB tf2zp decomposing an LPC-derived all-pole spectrum into minimum-phase filter H(z); computing the whitening filter for speech coding by factoring the LPC power spectrum; scipy.signal.lfilter designing causal minimum-phase filter from spectral envelope; Proakis Digital Signal Processing textbook example of factoring S(z) = 1/(1 - 0.81z^(-2)) into H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.9z^(-1)) | not: spectral analysis (which computes the PSD from a signal, the inverse direction); spectral decomposition (separating a signal into frequency bands, not factorizing the spectrum) [formal: factorizatio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: speech-codec
payload.scope: A human-made digital encoding standard that compresses speech audio for storage and transmission by modeling speech production parameters, enabling efficient bandwidth use in telephony and wireless communication systems.

definition.body: Speech-codec is a human-made digital encoding system that compresses speech signals by representing them with a compact set of parameters derived from a source-filter model of vocal tract production. Parameters: (1) the algorithm class — CELP (code-excited linear prediction), ACELP, or AMR-WB variant; (2) the bit rate — e.g. 8 kbps for ITU-T G.729, 12.2 kbps for GSM AMR, or 6.6 kbps for 3GPP EVRC; (3) the frame size — typically 10-30 ms; (4) the parameter vector — LPC/LSP coefficients, pitch lag, and codebook indices quantized per frame. The persistence mechanism is codified in ITU-T and 3GPP standards, implemented in telecom baseband chips and software SDKs, and deployed in billions of mobile devices for voice calls. e.g.: ITU-T G.729 Annex A 8 kbps CS-ACELP speech codec used in GSM VoIP; 3GPP AMR-WB 23.85 kbps codec in LTE voice calls; EVRC 7.95 kbps codec in CDMA2000 networks; Kaldi toolkit SGBF codec for research speech synthesis | not: audio-codec which compresses general audio beyond speech; speech-recognition which transcribes speech to text; speech-synthesis which generates speech from text [formal: codex vocis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-distortion
payload.scope: A human-made measure of dissimilarity between two spectral shapes, quantifying how different their frequency-domain energy distributions are from each other. Built to enable comparison, optimization, and error evaluation of spectral representations in speech processing, audio coding, and signal analysis.

definition.body: A spectral distortion is a human-made measure that quantifies the dissimilarity between two power spectra by computing a scalar value representing how much one spectral shape deviates from another. The computation: given two power spectra S1(f) and S2(f), a distortion metric D(S1,S2) is computed using a mathematical formula — common forms include the Itakura-Saito distance D_IS = integral(log(S1(f)/S2(f))) df + integral(S1(f)/S2(f)) df - N, the log-likelihood ratio distance D_LLR = integral(S1(f)/S2(f) - log(S1(f)/S2(f)) - 1) df, or the weighted cepstral distance computed on the cepstral coefficients of each spectrum. The result is a non-negative scalar: zero only when the two spectra are identical, increasing as their shapes diverge. Parameters: (1) the two spectra to compare, (2) the distortion metric formula, (3) optional weighting function across frequency bands. Persistence mechanism: encoded as standard functions in speech coding standards (ITU-T P.56 objective perceptual measure, ETSI AMR MOSNET), implemented in audio quality assessment libraries (Python pesq, VoiceMOS, PLCP), and used in codec optimization and speech quality evaluation. e.g.: Itakura-Saito distance between synthesized and target LPC spectra in ITU-T P.56 speech quality assessment; log-likelihood ratio distance between original and decoded spectra in GSM AMR codec evaluation; weighted spectral distortion in ETSI MOSNET measure for AMR voice quality scoring | not: cepstral-distance which operates only on cepstral coefficients rather than raw spectra; signal-to-noise ratio which compares signal power to noise power rather than spectral shape similarity; mean opinion score which is a subjective listening test not a spectral computation [formal: distortio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-decomposition
payload.scope: A human-made signal separation technique that decomposes a signal's spectrum into source and filter components using the cepstrum's quefrency-domain separation of rapidly-varying fine structure from slowly-varying spectral envelope. Built to enable independent processing, synthesis, and analysis of excitation and vocal-tract characteristics.

definition.body: A cepstrum-decomposition is a human-made signal processing technique that separates a signal's spectrum into source (excitation) and filter (transfer function) components by exploiting the quefrency-domain structure of the cepstrum. The procedure: (1) compute the power spectrum of the signal via FFT, (2) take the logarithm of each spectral magnitude, (3) apply the inverse FFT to obtain the cepstrum, (4) apply a window in the quefrency domain — a low-pass lifter isolates the slowly-varying filter component (low quefrency), while a high-pass lifter isolates the rapidly-varying source component (high quefrency), and (5) the inverse operation reconstructs each component in the frequency domain. Parameters: (1) the input signal, (2) the cepstrum length, (3) the lifter type (low-pass for filter extraction, high-pass for source extraction, all-pass for full decomposition), (4) the quefrency cutoff separating source from filter. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech synthesis toolkits (HTK, Kaldi source-filter processing), voice conversion systems (PSOLA, WORLD vocoder), and fault diagnosis pipelines for mechanical vibration analysis. e.g.: the WORLD vocoder's source-filter decomposition using cepstral analysis for voice conversion; HTK's cepstral liftering to extract vocal tract envelope from LPC analysis; Kaldi's cepstral decomposition pipeline for pitch detection in speech recognition; the quefrency-domain separation used in MTIA for rolling-centre removal in spectroscopic fault diagnosis | not: cepstrum (the transform itself, not the source-filter separation technique); inverse-filtering (which estimates filter coefficients directly without quefrency-domain windowing); cepstral-smoothing (which smooths coefficients rather than separating components) [formal: decompositio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-analysis
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing methodology that operates on cepstral representations to extract features for pattern recognition, classification, and reconstruction of signals. Built to enable pitch detection, speaker identification, speech recognition, and fault diagnosis through analysis of the quefrency-domain structure.

definition.body: A cepstrum-analysis is a human-made signal processing methodology that uses cepstral representations — the quefrency-domain transform of a signal's power spectrum — as the basis for feature extraction, pattern recognition, and signal reconstruction. The methodology comprises: (1) cepstrum computation (FFT → log-power spectrum → inverse FFT), (2) quefrency-domain operations (liftering, windowing, peak detection, smoothing, subtraction) applied to the cepstrum, (3) cepstral coefficient extraction (selecting subsets of quefrency-domain samples), and (4) application-specific interpretation (formant tracking, pitch estimation, spectral shape comparison). Parameters: (1) the input signal, (2) the window and overlap for frame-based analysis, (3) the FFT size, (4) the cepstral coefficients or operations selected, (5) the interpretation scheme for the resulting features. Persistence mechanism: standard methodology in speech recognition toolkits (Kaldi MFCC/PLP frontends, HTK feature extraction), audio analysis libraries (librosa cepstral functions), and diagnostic systems (vibration analysis, acoustic monitoring). e.g.: the Kaldi MFCC feature extraction pipeline using 13 cepstral coefficients from 25ms Hamming-windowed frames; the librosa.ceps function for computing discrete cosine transform-based cepstra in audio analysis; HTK cepstral analysis for formant tracking in speech synthesis; the cepstrum-based pitch detection in Praat for voice quality assessment | not: cepstrum (the transform itself, not the full methodology); linear-prediction (estimates filter coefficients without cepstral intermediate); spectral-analysis (operates directly on the frequency-domain representation) [formal: analasis cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-sequence
payload.scope: A human-made data structure representing the ordered sequence of cepstral coefficients indexed by quefrency position. Built to enable efficient storage, transmission, and manipulation of cepstral features for signal analysis, classification, and reconstruction.

definition.body: A cepstrum-sequence is a human-made ordered data structure containing cepstral coefficients indexed by their quefrency position, representing a signal's spectral structure in the quefrency domain. The sequence: c[0], c[1], ..., c[N-1] where each coefficient c[i] corresponds to one quefrency sample from the inverse FFT of the log-power spectrum. The coefficients are ordered by increasing quefrency: c[0] and c[1] capture the lowest quefrency components (gross spectral shape), intermediate coefficients capture formant-like structure, and higher-indexed coefficients resolve fine spectral detail and periodic structures. Parameters: (1) the input signal or its cepstrum, (2) the number of coefficients N (typically 8-40), (3) the normalization applied (mean, variance, or raw), (4) the coefficient type (DFT-based, DCT-based MFCC, or filterbank-based). Persistence mechanism: stored as fixed-length vectors in speech recognition feature files, transmitted in audio coding bitstreams, and processed as feature matrices in analysis libraries (Kaldi, librosa, HTK). e.g.: 13-dimensional cepstral sequence in Kaldi MFCC features; 20-coefficient cepstral sequence in HTK acoustic models; 39-coefficient sequence in VoiceMOS quality assessment; 13-coefficient sequence from librosa.feature.mfcc for audio classification | not: cepstral-sequence (the general feature representation, not the direct cepstrum output); cepstrum (the transform, not the coefficient array); cepstrum-decomposition (source-filter separation, not the coefficient array) [formal: series cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-smoothing
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing technique that applies smoothing in the cepstrum's quefrency domain to reduce noise and regularize spectral representations. Built to improve robustness of cepstral features for speech recognition, speaker identification, and audio classification.

definition.body: A cepstrum-smoothing is a human-made signal processing technique that reduces noise and suppresses fine spectral detail by applying a smoothing operation in the quefrency domain of the cepstrum. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the signal (FFT → log-power spectrum → inverse FFT), (2) apply a window function in the quefrency domain — typically a low-pass lifter that attenuates high-quefrency coefficients while preserving low-quefrency ones, or a rectangular window that truncates to a specified number of coefficients, and (3) optionally reconstruct the smoothed signal by exponentiating and applying the FFT. payload.name: cepstrum-domain
payload.scope: A human-made computational domain in which cepstral coefficients are the fundamental variables, with quefrency as the independent axis. Built to provide an alternative representation of signals where periodic spectral structure appears as peaks, enabling source-filter separation, pitch detection, and spectral shape analysis.

definition.body: A cepstrum-domain is a human-made computational domain where cepstral coefficients indexed by quefrency serve as the fundamental representation variables for signal analysis. In this domain, the independent axis is quefrency (measured in time-like units such as samples or milliseconds), and each point represents the amplitude of periodic spectral structure at a specific quefrency value. Low quefrency values encode the gross spectral envelope (formants, spectral tilt), intermediate values encode periodic spectral detail, and high values encode fine spectral texture and noise. definition.body: A cepstrum-domain is a human-made computational domain where cepstral coefficients indexed by quefrency serve as the fundamental representation variables for signal analysis. In this domain, the independent axis is quefrency (measured in time-like units such as samples or milliseconds), and each point represents the amplitude of periodic spectral structure at a specific quefrency value. Low quefrency values encode the gross spectral envelope (formants, spectral tilt), intermediate values encode periodic spectral detail, and high values encode fine spectral texture and noise. The domain is obtained by applying the inverse FFT to the log-power spectrum of a signal. Parameters: (1) the quefrency range and resolution (determined by FFT size), (2) the scaling convention (linear, dB, or normalized), (3) the boundary treatment (zero-padding, windowing). payload.name: cepstrum-distance
payload.scope: A human-made measure of dissimilarity between two signals computed directly from their cepstra, without converting to cepstral coefficients or other feature representations. Built to enable comparison of spectral shapes directly in the quefrency domain.

definition.body: A cepstrum-distance is a human-made measure of dissimilarity between two signals computed by comparing their cepstra directly in the quefrency domain. The computation: given two cepstra c1 and c2 obtained from the power spectra of two signals, a distance metric D(c1,c2) is computed — common forms include the L2 norm D = sqrt(sum((c1[i]-c2[i])^2)), the L1 norm D = sum(|c1[i]-c2[i]|), the cosine distance D = 1-cosine_similarity(c1,c2), or the weighted cepstral distance with frequency-dependent weights. The result is a non-negative scalar measuring how differently the two signals' spectra are structured. Parameters: (1) the two input signals or their cepstra, (2) the distance metric formula, (3) optional quefrency-range weighting, (4) the normalization applied to cepstra before comparison. Persistence mechanism: encoded in speech recognition and speaker verification systems as the core comparison metric for cepstral features, implemented in audio analysis libraries and used in quality assessment and anomaly detection. e.g.: L2 cepstrum distance in CMVN-normalized Kaldi features for speaker verification; cosine distance between cepstra in PLP-based speech recognition; weighted cepstrum distance in VoiceMOS quality estimation; L1 distance between cepstra for audio anomaly detection | not: cepstral-distance (which operates on cepstral coefficient vectors, not raw cepstra); signal-to-noise ratio (compares signal to noise power, not spectral shapes); cepstrum-smoothing (modifies, not compares cepstra) [formal: distantia cepstrum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: graph-neural-network
payload.scope: People made graph neural networks to learn representations of graph-structured data by propagating and transforming feature vectors across edges, enabling node classification, link prediction, and graph-level property estimation in domains like chemistry, social networks, and knowledge graphs.

definition.body: A graph neural network is a human-made neural architecture that operates on graph-structured data by iteratively updating node feature vectors through neighborhood aggregation. Each GNN layer computes new representations for node i by combining its current features with aggregated features from its neighbors: h_i^(l+1) = COMBINE(h_i^(l), AGGREGATE({h_j^(l) for j in N(i)})), where N(i) denotes the neighbor set, AGGREGATE is a permutation-invariant function (sum, mean, or max pooling), and COMBINE is a trainable transformation (concatenation followed by a neural layer). Message-passing propagates information across k hops in k layers. The network persists as saved model weights (e.g., PyTorch checkpoint files) and deployed inference services. e.g.: PyTorch Geometric GCN implementation on citation network node classification; DeepMind AlphaFold2 using equivariant graph networks for protein structure prediction; Stanford RGCN on Wikidata link prediction with 18 relation types; OpenGraphBERT pretraining on OpenGraph corpus of 10 billion edges | not: graph convolutional network restricted to spectral graph filters (a specific GNN variant, not the general class); recurrent neural network operating on sequential data (no graph topology); graph autoencoder (an architecture pattern using GNNs as encoder, not the GNN class itself) [formal: rete neuralis graphalis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

replacementSpec.body: A graph is a human-made visual construct that encodes data values as geometric elements (points, lines, bars, areas) on one or more axes for quantitative comparison. Parameters: (1) the encoded variables and the axes or scales they sit on; (2) the geometric element and the mapping that assigns it to a data value; (3) the encoding, which preserves the data's structure so that patterns, trends and relationships are readable at a glance. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard visual grammar of statistics and data visualization — named chart types (bar chart, line graph, box plot, scatter plot) taught in curricula and maintained as canonical implementations in plotting libraries (matplotlib, ggplot2, d3.js) and in the charts of reports and dashboards. e.g.: a bar chart comparing quarterly revenue in a financial report; a line graph of daily temperatures from a weather station; the box plot of response times in a performance dashboard | not: a graph-theoretic graph (a vertex-edge structure studied as a mathematical object, not data plotted on axes); a flowchart of a manufacturing procedure (its subject is the process steps, not data values on axes) [formal: graphus | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
